body.text: In short:
Israeli opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot has described arson attacks on Palestinian villages in the occupied West Bank as Jewish terrorism.
Settlers set fire to vehicles and homes in several villages in the early hours of Sunday.
What's next?
Mr Eisenkot called for those responsible to be arrested and for "severe sanctions" to be imposed on them.

Gadi Eisenkot, who is Israel Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's main rival, has described arson attacks on Palestinian villages in the occupied West Bank as "Jewish terrorism in every sense of the word".
Settlers set fire to vehicles and homes in several Palestinian villages overnight, drawing one of the sharpest condemnations yet from the politician charged with forming Israel's next government.

Twelve vehicles were reportedly set alight in at least five villages in the early hours of Sunday, local time, with images and videos showing burning cars in Kafr Malik, Deir as Sudan and Deir Abu Mashal. Homes were also reportedly set alight in villages in northern West Bank, including Deir Ballut.
It comes as settler attacks have surged in recent months in the West Bank.
Many rights groups and Netanyahu's rivals blame the approach of his government to settlement expansion, led by far-right members of the coalition, for encouraging violent settlers.

In Kafr Malik, seven cars were set alight. Videos obtained by the ABC from residents show people rushing to put out huge flames engulfing multiple vehicles in the early hours of the morning. Residents said they feared for their lives.
The ABC spoke to Montaser Almalki in Kafr Malik, who woke to the sound of explosions just a few metres from his home.
"When you wake up at 2:30 in the morning to seven cars on fire, the sight is terrifying. It's frightening for adults and children alike … it's an awful sight," Mr Almalki said.
He said there was screaming and panic in the village as he rushed to get water to extinguish the fire.

Graffiti was sprayed in the area, including the phrases "Hit them hard", "Revenge" and "Don't mess with the people of Israel". One wall read "Greetings from Susya", an apparent reference to a recently evacuated Israeli outpost in the southern West Bank.
"There are also threatening slogans aimed at us … they do this to spread terror and fear in people's hearts,"
Mr Amalki said.

He said it was not the first arson attack in the village, citing an attack in June 2025, but said the distance to the outposts usually meant there were fewer attacks in this area, which he had considered a safe neighbourhood.
Eisenkot calls for arrests

Writing on X, Mr Eisenkot said sabotage by extremist groups that set fire to vehicles and homes "undermines regional stability, endangers lives and severely damages the national security and foreign relations of the state of Israel".

He called for those responsible to be arrested and for "severe sanctions" to be imposed on them. He blamed the escalation on Netanyahu's government, including far-right ministers Itamar Ben-Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich.
Israeli soldiers and Border Police were sent to four of the villages, according to a post by the authorities on X.
Police said they were investigating who set the fires and sprayed the graffiti. No arrests had been reported.
Rights groups say authorities enable attacks
The Israeli military condemned the violence, but human rights organisations said settler attacks were enabled by the authorities and the wider system.
B'Tselem spokesperson Yair Dvir said: "At the moment, we don't see any real attempts by the Israeli authorities to stop it. A condemnation is not enough."

The attacks follow a deadly olive harvest season and a surge in settler violence. The UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs says there have been an average of six settler attacks a day in the West Bank in 2026.
An ABC analysis found as many as 30 incidents of violence were recorded some days, including Israeli military raids and settler attacks.
Last week, Australia sanctioned three individuals for illegal settlement expansion and human rights abuses against Palestinians in the West Bank.
The latest sanctions follow measures against two ministers in the Netanyahu government in July last year: National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir and Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich.

Australia and other countries have raised concerns about the surge in violence by settlers against the Palestinian community in recent years, which has hit record levels according to organisations such as the United Nations.
The Netanyahu government has been accused of allowing the violence to spread and minimising its severity by claiming it is being perpetrated by a handful of young men from broken homes.
"They give them almost total impunity and this is one of the ways how the Israeli system is actually supporting and allowing those attacks to continue,"
Mr Dvir said.
We cannot continue to treat the violations and the attack as separate phenomenon … there is a system behind it."
Critics say Mr Eisenkot may not be much different if he succeeds in forming a government within the next fortnight.

"If you really listen to what Eisenkot says and what the other members of the change government says, they are actually against the Palestinian state, and they are in favour of the project of settlements in general. So we do not really believe that they will try to change the policy," Mr Dvir said.
Settlements and informal settlements, known as outposts, are Jewish communities built on Palestinian land. The Israeli government has legalised more than 100 settlements since late 2022.
All settlements are illegal under international law.
The International Court of Justice reinforced this in July 2024, with a landmark advisory opinion telling Israel to end its unlawful presence "as rapidly as possible".
For Palestinians in the West Bank, change could not come soon enough.
"The one place that was safe for you was your home. And when the fire reaches your home, then even in your home you're not safe,"
Mr Almalki said.
ABC
